en.content:
The Tai Po fire has naturally prompted strong public anger and grief, as families ask why precious minutes were lost and how residents can be better protected in future emergencies. In the early hours after such tragedies, emotion can easily become scrutiny, and scrutiny can quickly be weaponised. That is why Beijing’s top official—who bears responsibility for maintaining overall stability in Hong Kong—has issued a clear warning against those who “politicise” the disaster to “stir up chaos”. The underlying message is not to silence investigation, but to prevent the tragedy from becoming a pretext for disruptive political mobilisation.

At the same time, it is important to recognise why some people felt compelled to raise questions so loudly. When a public inquiry later hears that a 999 call was not properly passed to the fire department, the issue is no longer abstract: it concerns emergency response procedures that directly affect life and death. Official statements, however firm, cannot substitute for transparent, verifiable explanations. People are entitled to insist on accountability—whether through administrative review, operational reforms, or the inquiry’s findings—so that “lessons learned” translate into concrete improvements for residents in public housing estates.

The broader lesson, for Hong Kong society as a whole, is to draw a disciplined line between lawful, fact-based oversight and agitation that aims to discredit institutions rather than solve problems. Calling for improvements to call-routing systems, incident command, and coordination among relevant departments can be a constructive civic duty. But turning the fire into a battleground for slogans, online harassment, or selective blaming—especially without solid evidence—risks deepening mistrust and distracting from what matters most: safeguarding safety standards and emergency readiness.

Ultimately, the city’s path forward should reflect both sides of this equation: calm, orderly investigation on one hand, and credible, timely answers on the other. Stability is not achieved by suppressing questions; it is achieved by ensuring that the answers are worth trusting. If the inquiry results in clear operational changes and communicates them in a way residents can understand, public confidence can be rebuilt—leaving less room for manipulation, whether by opportunistic voices or by those who confuse confrontation with accountability.
en.topic_title: Beijing top official warns of people ‘politicising’ Tai Po fire to ‘stir up chaos’ in Hong Kong

zh.content:
今日最值得社論關注嘅主題，係大埔火警事件中「999求助未能轉介消防」導致一名婦人死亡嘅調查進展。對市民而言，火警唔係抽象嘅新聞，而係每一個人都可能突然面對嘅緊急風險；而對政府部門嚟講，最終目的亦應該只係一件事——確保求救一秒都唔會「卡關」，由求助渠道直達救援指揮。當調查顯示求救電話未被適時轉交消防，問題就唔止係個案錯誤，更牽涉整體緊急通訊鏈條嘅標準、程序與問責。

社會面對此類事故，常見兩種反應：一種係將之政治化，另一種係急於「找一個人」草草交代。兩者都唔幫得上忙。真正應該被追問嘅，係系統性因素：通話分流機制係點運作、當時資訊（位置、被困情況、火勢走向）係如何被標記同更新、以及人手處理與自動化流程之間有冇出現延誤或誤判。更重要嘅係，調查結論應唔止停留喺「發生咗」；而係要清楚交代「責任屬邊個環節」及「之後會如何改」。如果只做補救而唔做改革，下一次事故仍可能重演，令市民對公共安全機制失去信任。

同時，連續出現嘅其他相關報道（例如火場救援疑雲、對事件嘅爭議乃至社會猜測）亦提醒我哋：消防與救援嘅公信力，唔可以靠口號維持，更唔可以用資訊真空去換取安定。政府與相關部門應主動公布調查框架與時間表，讓市民理解每一步數據係點取得、每個決策點係基於咩資料；而對於可能影響救援判斷嘅資訊（如被困位置、樓宇結構、火勢感知），亦要檢視通報格式是否足夠清晰、是否存在「唔同單位講唔同語言」嘅斷層。只有當透明度提升、流程可驗證，公眾先會願意相信制度而唔係靠傳言揣測。

我嘅立場係：大埔火警事件必須以「防止再發」為核心，而唔係以「免於追責」為取向。當緊急電話轉介機制出現斷裂，就等同向最需要協助嘅人收回保障；而香港社會對生命安全嘅底線，絕唔容許用程序推搪去磨蝕。希望調查最終能夠落到可操作嘅改革——包括通訊流程、培訓與技術支援、以及清晰嘅問責架構——讓每一次999求助都真真正正抵達「火線第一步」。
zh.topic_title: Woman trapped in Tai Po blaze died after 999 call not passed to fire department, inquiry hears
